FOUNDERS' AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

FOUNDERS' EQUITY SPLIT
Acme, Inc.'s founding equity is allocated among its founders as follows, expressed as a percentage of Acme, Inc.'s fully-diluted equity as of the effective date of this agreement:

Jordan Morgan: 50%
Casey Lee: 50%

Total: 100%

This allocation reflects the founders' agreement as of the date below and is subject to the vesting schedule referenced separately in this agreement, any subsequent equity issuances (including to new hires, advisors, or investors), and the governing documents of whatever entity Acme, Inc. is or becomes (articles or certificate of incorporation and bylaws, or articles of organization and an operating agreement, as applicable).

VESTING SCHEDULE
Each founder's equity in Acme, Inc. described above is subject to the following vesting schedule, unless marked as fully vested at grant:

Vesting commencement date: September 1, 2026
Total vesting period: 48 months
Cliff period, if any: 12 months
Vesting frequency after the cliff: ☐ monthly ☐ quarterly ☐ annually ☐ other: _________________
Treatment on voluntary departure before full vesting: _________________
Treatment on involuntary termination before full vesting: _________________
Treatment on a change of control of Acme, Inc., including any acceleration: _________________

The blanks above control; this document does not set a default vesting structure for Acme, Inc.

TAX TREATMENT OF FOUNDER STOCK SUBJECT TO VESTING
When a founder receives stock or another form of equity in Acme, Inc. that is subject to a vesting schedule, federal tax law generally does not tax that equity's value at the time of grant. Instead, the value is included in the founder's taxable income later — in the year the equity becomes vested or freely transferable, based on its fair market value at that later time, not its value at grant. This is the default rule; it applies unless the founder makes a timely election under a separate provision of the same statute, described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If, in connection with the performance of services, property is transferred to any person other than the person for whom such services are performed, the excess of— (1) the fair market value of such property (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse) at the first time the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever occurs earlier, over (2) the amount (if any) paid for such property, shall be included in the gross income of the person who performed such services in the first taxable year in which the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever is applicable. The preceding sentence shall not apply if such person sells or otherwise disposes of such property in an arm's length transaction before his rights in such property become transferable or not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 83(a), Internal Revenue Code, general rule for property transferred in connection with performance of services (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/83)
  Known gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 83(a)) and applies the same way regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation or this agreement — it is a separate body of law from the state-law rules on entity formation and fiduciary duty addressed elsewhere in this document. This clause states the general default rule only; it does not determine the fair market value of any specific grant of equity, which is a factual question this clause does not resolve. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 83(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT MAKES EQUITY "SUBJECT TO VESTING" FOR TAX PURPOSES
The same federal statute that governs when vesting equity is taxed also defines the condition that makes equity count as subject to vesting in the first place: a "substantial risk of forfeiture." Equity meets that test when the founder's right to keep it fully is conditioned on that founder performing future services for Acme, Inc. — the same structure a typical multi-year, service-based vesting schedule uses. Whether a specific grant of equity meets this statutory test is a question of fact about how that particular grant is structured, not a label this document assigns.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The rights of a person in property are subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture if such person's rights to full enjoyment of such property are conditioned upon the future performance of substantial services by any individual."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 83(c)(1), Internal Revenue Code, definition of "substantial risk of forfeiture" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/83)
  Known gap: This is one subsection of the same federal statute cited in the clause above (26 U.S.C. § 83) — not an independent source, and disclosed as such. It is federal law and applies regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation. This clause defines the statutory test only; it does not determine whether any particular equity grant satisfies it.

THE SECTION 83(B) ELECTION AND ITS 30-DAY DEADLINE
Federal tax law allows a person who receives equity subject to vesting to elect to be taxed on that equity's value at the time of grant instead of waiting until it vests. This is commonly called an "83(b) election," after the statutory subsection that creates it. If made, the general vesting-based timing rule described above does not apply to that equity, and if the equity is later forfeited before it vests, no tax deduction is allowed for the amount that was already included in income because of the election. An 83(b) election, if made, must be filed not later than 30 days after the date the equity is transferred, and once made, it cannot be revoked except with the consent of the IRS.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any person who performs services in connection with which property is transferred to any person may elect to include in his gross income for the taxable year in which such property is transferred, the excess of— (A) the fair market value of such property at the time of transfer (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse), over (B) the amount (if any) paid for such property. If such election is made, subsection (a) shall not apply with respect to the transfer of such property, and if such property is subsequently forfeited, no deduction shall be allowed in respect of such forfeiture. (2) Election An election under paragraph (1) with respect to any transfer of property shall be made in such manner as the Secretary prescribes and shall be made not later than 30 days after the date of such transfer. Such election may not be revoked except with the consent of the Secretary."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 83(b), Internal Revenue Code, election to include property's value in gross income in the year of transfer (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/83)
  "Time for making election. Except as provided in the following sentence, the election referred to in paragraph (a) of this section shall be filed not later than 30 days after the date the property was transferred (or, if later, January 29, 1970) and may be filed prior to the date of transfer. Any statement filed before February 15, 1970, which was amended not later than February 16, 1970, in order to make it conform to the requirements of paragraph (e) of this section, shall be deemed a proper election under section 83(b)."
  — Treas. Reg. § 1.83-2(b), Treasury Regulations, time for making a section 83(b) election (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.83-2)
  Known gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 83(b)) and applies the same way regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation or this agreement. The regulation cited alongside the statute below independently restates the same 30-day deadline — the two sources are not fully independent of each other on that specific point, since the regulation implements the statute, and that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as two unrelated confirmations. The regulation's text also carries a parenthetical referencing "January 29, 1970," a leftover from when the regulation was first adopted; it has no effect on a transfer occurring now, since any current transfer date is later than that fixed 1970 date, leaving the 30-day rule as the operative deadline. Separately, the regulation (not quoted in full here) also specifies required content for the election statement and requires copies to be delivered to the company — procedural detail this clause does not restate. This document does not itself file an election with the IRS or track whether one has been filed; it states the deadline as a matter of law only.

WORK-FOR-HIRE BASELINE FOR FOUNDER-CREATED IP
Work a founder creates for Acme, Inc. within the scope of an actual employment relationship with Acme, Inc. is generally owned by Acme, Inc. automatically, under the "work made for hire" doctrine — the same default that applies to any employee's work product. That default depends on the founder actually being an employee under the law's test, not on titles: courts weigh factors including who controls the manner and means of the work, who supplies tools and workspace, how the work is paid for, and whether the person receives employee benefits and employee tax treatment. Work created outside an actual employment relationship — including by a founder acting as a contractor, advisor, or in some other non-employee capacity — is not automatically owned by Acme, Inc. under this doctrine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 201(b), U.S. Code, ownership of work made for hire (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201)
  "In determining whether a hired party is an employee under the general common law of agency, we consider the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which the product is accomplished."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  "Some factors, therefore, will often have little or no significance in determining whether a party is an independent contractor or an employee. In contrast, there are some factors that will be significant in virtually every situation. These include: (1) the hiring party's right to control the manner and means of creation; (2) the skill required; (3) the provision of employee benefits; (4) the tax treatment of the hired party; and (5) whether the hiring party has the right to assign additional projects to the hired party. These factors will almost always be relevant and should be given more weight in the analysis, because they will usually be highly probative of the true nature of the employment relationship."
  — Aymes v. Bonelli, 980 F.2d 857 (2d Cir. 1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/596113/clifford-scott-aymes-v-jonathan-bonelli-doing-business-as-island-swimming/)
  Known gap: This clause restates, for the founder context, the same federal copyright doctrine and the same primary-source quotes already verified in this project's Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement document (reused verbatim, not re-fetched, per this project's source-reuse practice). It does not by itself resolve the separate question — addressed in the next clause — of work a founder created before a specific company existed as a legal entity.

PRE-INCORPORATION AND PRE-SIGNING WORK IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION
Work a founder created before Acme, Inc. existed as a legal entity, or before this agreement was signed, is not automatically transferred to Acme, Inc. by the work-for-hire doctrine described above. That doctrine turns on an actual employer-employee relationship existing at the time the work was created, and an entity that had not yet been formed cannot have been anyone's employer during that period. Ownership of work created before Acme, Inc.'s formation generally remains with the individual founder who created it unless and until that founder expressly assigns it — assignment does not happen automatically just because the founder later joins, works for, or holds equity in Acme, Inc.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In spite of the fact that Fincke, as the named inventor on the '645 Application, was the de facto owner of the invention disclosed in the '645 Application and any patent to be issued, no licensing agreement was ever entered into between Fincke and Access regarding Access's use of the intellectual property."
  — Access Cardiosystems, Inc. v. Fincke (In re Access Cardiosystems, Inc.), 340 B.R. 127 (Bankr. D. Mass. 2006) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1851772/access-cardiosystems-inc-v-fincke-in-re-acces-cardiosystems-inc/)
  Known gap: This point follows from the definition of "employer" already built into the work-for-hire doctrine cited in the clause above (17 U.S.C. § 101/201(b) and the Reid agency test) — it is not an independently codified California or federal rule specifically addressing pre-incorporation founder IP, and no such distinct statute or clean holding was found in this research. One federal bankruptcy court decision illustrates the practical stakes: in a dispute where a founder had developed the underlying invention before the company was incorporated and never signed an assignment, the company had to establish ownership through a fact-intensive fiduciary-duty and conduct-based theory rather than automatic operation of law. That case arose under patent law, not copyright — patent law has no work-for-hire doctrine of its own, so the case is not a patent-law analog to the copyright rule described above; it is offered only as a general illustration of the practical risk an unsigned assignment creates when ownership of pre-formation work is later disputed. That case also did not apply California law — it involved a Delaware corporation and was decided by a Massachusetts federal bankruptcy court — so it is offered here only as an illustration of that risk, not as California authority or as a general rule that pre-incorporation IP is always the founder's personal property. This is a single case; no additional independent source was found for this specific illustration.

WHICH FIDUCIARY-DUTY STATUTE APPLIES DEPENDS ON HOW FOUNDERS HAVE ORGANIZED
Founders do not owe each other the same fiduciary duties automatically, regardless of what business structure they use — which statute applies depends on the entity form chosen. If founders are operating as a general partnership (including, potentially, by default before any formal entity is created), each partner owes a statutory duty of loyalty and a duty of care to the partnership and the other partners. If founders instead form a corporation, that partnership statute does not apply to them as founders — a corporation's directors instead owe duties defined by a separate statute governing corporate directors, requiring good faith, a reasonable belief that their actions serve the corporation's and shareholders' best interests, and the care an ordinarily prudent person would use in a like position. If founders form an LLC, a third, separate statute applies: in a member-managed LLC, members owe a duty of loyalty and duty of care similar in structure to the partnership duties; in a manager-managed LLC, those duties shift to the manager or managers, and a member who is not also a manager owes no fiduciary duty to the company or the other members solely because of being a member.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(a), California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the two fiduciary duties a partner owes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16404.)
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(a), California General Corporation Law, a director's standard of conduct (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  "In a manager-managed limited liability company, all of the following rules apply: (1) Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members. (2) Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers. (3) Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(f), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: These are three genuinely separate California statutes, each addressing a different entity form — that separation is disclosed here rather than treated as one combined rule. Each is one state's statute, offered as evidence of California's default structure for the relevant entity type — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific company, and not a determination of which entity form a specific company has actually chosen. The partnership and LLC citations below were previously verified for this project's Partnership Agreement and LLC Operating Agreement documents and are reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched; the corporate-director citation was independently fetched and verified for this document. This clause does not resolve which entity type applies to a specific group of founders, and does not address the fact-specific question of whether founders who have not yet formed any entity might be treated as a de facto general partnership under California law before formal organization — that determination depends on facts this clause does not evaluate.

A FOUNDER'S STATUS AS AN EMPLOYEE IS STILL AT-WILL BY DEFAULT
When a founder also works for Acme, Inc. as an employee — common in early-stage companies — California's default employment rule still applies to that role: employment with no specified term may be ended by either party, on notice to the other, at any time and without cause. Founder status, equity ownership, or a title such as "co-founder" does not by itself change this default. The default can be modified only by an express or implied agreement establishing enforceable expectations about the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination; absent such an agreement, the at-will default controls.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2922, California Labor Code, at-will employment default (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2922.)
  "Pursuant to Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary, the relationship is terminable at any time without cause. But when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, Labor Code section 2922 does not diminish the force of such contractual or legal obligations. The presumption that an employment relationship of indefinite duration is intended to be terminable at will is therefore "subject, like any presumption, to contrary evidence. This may take the form of an agreement, express or implied, that . . . the employment relationship will continue indefinitely, pending the occurrence of some event such as the employer's dissatisfaction with the employee's services or the existence of some 'cause' for termination.""
  — Foley v. Interactive Data Corp., 47 Cal.3d 654 (1988) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1170824/foley-v-interactive-data-corp/)
  Known gap: This is one state's default employment rule (Cal. Labor Code § 2922) and applies only to a founder's separate status as an employee of a specific company, not to that founder's equity ownership or governance rights, which are addressed elsewhere in this document. The case cited alongside the statute discusses and applies the same statutory section, so its first quoted passage is not fully independent of the statute on that narrow point — that overlap is disclosed here. The case's second quoted passage adds genuinely separate content: it is itself quoting a different, earlier California Court of Appeal decision (Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc., 116 Cal.App.3d 311) to describe how the at-will presumption can be rebutted by an implied agreement, based on factors such as personnel policies, an employee's length of service, and employer assurances of continued employment — this clause does not evaluate whether such factors are present in any specific case.

SIGNATURES
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the undersigned founders of Acme, Inc. have executed this Founders' Agreement as of the date last signed below.

Jordan Morgan
Signature: ☐ _________________________
Date: _______________

Casey Lee
Signature: ☐ _________________________
Date: _______________

If founders instead form a corporation, that partnership statute does not apply to them as founders — a corporation's directors instead owe duties defined by a separate statute governing corporate directors, requiring good faith, a reasonable belief that their actions serve the corporation's and shareholders' best interests, and the care an ordinarily prudent person would use in a like position. If founders form an LLC, a third, separate statute applies: in a member-managed LLC, members owe a duty of loyalty and duty of care similar in structure to the partnership duties; in a manager-managed LLC, those duties shift to the manager or managers, and a member who is not also a manager owes no fiduciary duty to the company or the other members solely because of being a member.

citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the two fiduciary duties a partner owes
citations.quote: (a) The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c).

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a director's standard of conduct
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC
citations.quote: In a manager-managed limited liability company, all of the following rules apply: (1) Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members. (2) Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers. (3) Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member.

expectedJSON.gap: These are three genuinely separate California statutes, each addressing a different entity form — that separation is disclosed here rather than treated as one combined rule. Each is one state's statute, offered as evidence of California's default structure for the relevant entity type — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific company, and not a determination of which entity form a specific company has actually chosen. The partnership and LLC citations below were previously verified for this project's Partnership Agreement and LLC Operating Agreement documents and are reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched; the corporate-director citation was independently fetched and verified for this document. This clause does not resolve which entity type applies to a specific group of founders, and does not address the fact-specific question of whether founders who have not yet formed any entity might be treated as a de facto general partnership under California law before formal organization — that determination depends on facts this clause does not evaluate.

expectedJSON.body: When a founder also works for Acme, Inc. as an employee — common in early-stage companies — California's default employment rule still applies to that role: employment with no specified term may be ended by either party, on notice to the other, at any time and without cause. Founder status, equity ownership, or a title such as "co-founder" does not by itself change this default. The default can be modified only by an express or implied agreement establishing enforceable expectations about the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination; absent such an agreement, the at-will default controls.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, at-will employment default
citations.quote: An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month.

Pursuant to Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary, the relationship is terminable at any time without cause. But when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, Labor Code section 2922 does not diminish the force of such contractual or legal obligations. The presumption that an employment relationship of indefinite duration is intended to be terminable at will is therefore "subject, like any presumption, to contrary evidence. This may take the form of an agreement, express or implied, that . . . the employment relationship will continue indefinitely, pending the occurrence of some event such as the employer's dissatisfaction with the employee's services or the existence of some 'cause' for termination."

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's default employment rule (Cal. Labor Code § 2922) and applies only to a founder's separate status as an employee of a specific company, not to that founder's equity ownership or governance rights, which are addressed elsewhere in this document. The case cited alongside the statute discusses and applies the same statutory section, so its first quoted passage is not fully independent of the statute on that narrow point — that overlap is disclosed here. The case's second quoted passage adds genuinely separate content: it is itself quoting a different, earlier California Court of Appeal decision (Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc., 116 Cal.App.3d 311) to describe how the at-will presumption can be rebutted by an implied agreement, based on factors such as personnel policies, an employee's length of service, and employer assurances of continued employment — this clause does not evaluate whether such factors are present in any specific case.
